# D&D 5.5e: Universal Edition

## Unofficial Homebrew Playtest Rulebook — Covenant Engine v1.0

This is a complete campaign engine for Universal. It uses a familiar fifth-edition d20 chassis while rebuilding the parts that need to carry investigation, horror, social consequence, living factions, divine pressure, ancient eras, industrial play, planetary travel, and interstellar play. The attached twenty-two Universal class dossiers remain the authority for class features. This book supplies the shared rules those classes use.

Universal is warm, wet, crowded, engineered, divine, rotten, and hungry. Its gods are creators, predators, patrons, prisoners, and sources of Ichor. Its people are not defined by their creators. Its campaign future is not defined by an outline. The rules therefore make choices legible and consequential without using mechanics to force a choice.

> Core promise. The world reacts honestly. The gods may tempt, threaten, bargain, or collect a price. Factions may remember and retaliate. Alignment may record a pattern. None of those things chooses a player character's action for them.

# 1. The Covenant Engine

## 1.1 What this system keeps

The system keeps the parts of modern fifth-edition fantasy play that make characters readable and portable: six ability scores, d20 tests, proficiency bonus, Armor Class, hit points, Hit Dice, saving throws, spell ranks 1–9, concentration, resistance, vulnerability, class levels, subclasses, feats, and the level 1–20 proficiency curve.

It also keeps the existing Universal class contract. Every class has a hit die, primary abilities, two saving throw proficiencies, a canonical deity, a Bounty Ichor reserve, a core class engine, and three paths: melee/non-caster, half-caster, and full-caster. A class dossier wins if a specific feature conflicts with a general rule in this book.

## 1.2 What this system changes

The Covenant Engine adds or replaces the following shared procedures.

| Need | Universal rule |
|---|---|
| More expressive d20 results | Five outcome bands, declared stakes, and an optional Push |
| Flexible turns | Three Beats plus one Reaction, with a compatibility translation for action and bonus-action features |
| Better investigations | Essential clues are found by competent approaches; rolls decide speed, clarity, safety, and extra leverage |
| Player-facing moral growth | Eight behavioral axes, Convictions, Ties, Resolve, Strain, Resonance, and Divine Claim |
| Horror without loss-of-agency caricatures | Composure, Stress, Fractures, and player-authored Scars |
| Living threats and projects | Visible or concealed 4-, 6-, 8-, and 12-segment clocks |
| Play across history and space | Era and Scale tags that change access and fiction without rewriting core math |
| Meaningful armor and defenses | AC prevents hits; Guard lets armor absorb a limited amount of harm |
| Less arbitrary death | A Session Zero lethality mode and explicit Last Threshold choices |
| Campaign autonomy | Hooks, redundant lore, multiple approaches, open resolutions, and honest consequence |

## 1.3 Design genealogy

This game borrows the purpose of useful mechanics, then implements that purpose in its own way.

| Source tradition | Purpose retained | Covenant Engine implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Fifth-edition fantasy | Fast d20 familiarity, bounded numbers, class identity | Familiar statistics, PB curve, AC/HP, saves, spells, and levels |
| Tactical d20 fantasy | Flexible action use, degrees of outcome, clear modes of play | Three Beats, outcome bands, and Scene Modes |
| Investigative horror | Clues, escalating risk, pushes, long-term psychological cost | Clue-forward tests, Pushes, Composure, Fractures, and Scars |
| Narrative heroic fantasy | Spotlight fairness, player currency, clocks, identity phrases | Spotlight checks, Resolve, clocks, Convictions, Ties, and Experiences |

No rule requires dice when the result is certain or when failure would add nothing. Say yes, state the cost, or ask for a test only when the outcome can change the situation.

## 1.4 Rules priority

Apply rules in this order:

1. The group's Session Zero agreements and safety boundaries.
2. A specific class, ancestry, spell, item, creature, or scene rule.
3. This core rulebook.
4. A fifth-edition-compatible source converted using Chapter 20.
5. A fair table ruling that is recorded if it will recur.

A later canon package supersedes an older one on the same subject. For this edition, the Eight-Axis Covenant Alignment package supersedes older four-axis alignment text inside the life compendium. The newest twenty-two-class package governs classes. Current pantheon and race JSON governs names, creator categories, and deity relationships. Geographic coordinates and specific public-transport routes are not rules in this edition.

# 2. Core Resolution

## 2.1 Tests

When an action is uncertain, risky, and consequential, make a test:

**d20 + ability modifier + proficiency, if trained + other modifiers**

The GM names the ability and the target number. The player names the approach. If a skill, tool, vehicle, language, profession, or field of study clearly supports the approach, proficiency applies. Expertise adds proficiency a second time. Proficiency is never added more than twice.

The standard ability scores remain Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

## 2.2 Difficulty numbers

| Difficulty | DC | Use |
|---|---:|---|
| Routine under pressure | 8 | A trained person should usually succeed |
| Standard | 12 | A capable person has a fair chance |
| Demanding | 16 | Training or a strong ability matters |
| Severe | 20 | Specialists are tested |
| Extraordinary | 24 | Exceptional preparation is expected |
| Legendary | 28 | A defining feat with rare leverage |
| Mythic | 32 | Possible only through epic power, ideal conditions, or sacrifice |

Do not increase a DC merely because a character is high level. Increase it when the task itself is harder. A locked household door does not become legendary because a level-17 hero touches it.

## 2.3 Outcome bands

For attacks, a natural 20 is a critical hit and a natural 1 misses. For other tests, use the total and the fiction.

| Result | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Total exceeds DC by 10+, or natural 20 when a breakthrough is possible | Breakthrough: success plus a strong benefit, speed, information, position, or reduced cost |
| Total meets or exceeds DC | Clean success: achieve the stated intent |
| Total misses by 1–4 | Costly opening: the GM offers success with a stated cost, reduced effect, delay, exposure, or hard choice; the player may accept or decline |
| Total misses by 5–9 | Setback: the intent fails or succeeds only in a sharply limited way, and the situation changes |
| Total misses by 10+, or natural 1 when a crisis is possible | Crisis: a serious consequence follows from the established risk; it never invents an unrelated punishment |

A natural 20 cannot accomplish something impossible, and a natural 1 does not make a competent character forget ordinary knowledge. Natural results change the band only when a breakthrough or crisis makes sense.

## 2.4 Stakes before dice

Before a consequential roll, establish four things in plain language:

1. Intent: what the character wants.
2. Approach: how they pursue it.
3. Effect: what success can accomplish.
4. Risk: what can happen if the attempt goes badly.

The GM must reveal unavoidable or character-altering risks. Hidden facts can remain hidden, but the player should know the kind of danger being accepted.

## 2.5 Edge and Burden

Edge represents favorable circumstances. Burden represents unfavorable circumstances.

- With one net Edge, roll 2d20 and keep the higher.
- With two net Edge, roll 3d20 and keep the highest.
- With one net Burden, roll 2d20 and keep the lower.
- With two net Burden, roll 3d20 and keep the lowest.
- Each Edge cancels one Burden. The maximum net rating is two.

Class features that grant advantage grant one Edge. Features that grant disadvantage grant one Burden. If a feature says a creature has advantage despite disadvantage, it sets the result to one Edge unless the feature says otherwise.

## 2.6 Assistance and group tests

To Assist, describe a distinct contribution and possess relevant access, training, or leverage. The acting character gains one Edge. A helper shares any direct consequence that logically reaches the attempt.

For a group test, everyone rolls only when each person's performance matters. The group succeeds if at least half succeed; a Breakthrough counts as two successes and a Crisis subtracts one success. If one specialist can lead while others support, use one test with Assistance instead.

## 2.7 Resolve

Resolve is a player's limited authority to reinforce what matters to their character. Each character can hold up to 3 Resolve.

Gain 1 Resolve when you willingly accept a meaningful complication or cost created by a Conviction, Duty, Tie, Temptation, or divine offer. The choice must change the scene; repeating harmless behavior does not generate Resolve.

Spend 1 Resolve to do one of the following:

- Add 1d6 after seeing a d20 total but before the outcome is narrated.
- Reduce incoming Stress by 2.
- Refuse a Divine Claim complication that would otherwise require a cost, when the covenant rules allow resistance.
- Declare a modest, plausible preparation tied to a proficiency, Experience, or earlier action.
- Keep the spotlight long enough to complete one linked action when interruption would make the scene incoherent.

## 2.8 Push

After a failed non-attack test, the player may Push once if they describe a new effort, sacrifice, tool, angle, or escalation. The GM states a stronger consequence before the reroll. Roll again with one Edge and use the new result. A Push cannot be rerolled, and Resolve may modify it only if the declared consequence remains meaningful.

Pushes are never required to obtain an essential clue. They are for speed, completeness, leverage, rescue, concealment, or avoiding a consequence.

## 2.9 Experiences

Each character writes two short Experience phrases at creation, such as “Raised in a Reef Court,” “Former Prison-Engine Inspector,” or “Never Abandon Chosen Family.” An Experience is broader than a skill but narrower than a personality.

Once per scene, when an Experience materially changes the approach, the player may either gain one Edge before the roll or add +2 after rolling. An Experience improves to +3 at level 9 and +4 at level 17. It never replaces a required tool, language, physical capability, or specific training.

# 3. Character Creation

## 3.1 Creation sequence

1. Agree on campaign frame, era, starting level, lethality, and safety boundaries.
2. Choose a people, parent race, bloodline or lineage where applicable, and cultural upbringing.
3. Choose a background and two Experiences.
4. Assign ability scores.
5. Choose one of the twenty-two Universal classes and its path plan.
6. Record the class's canonical deity, Bounty Ichor trigger, Practices, and Hazards.
7. Choose Convictions, Ties, and initial alignment scores.
8. Choose proficiencies, languages, tools, equipment, and era permissions.
9. Calculate defenses, Guard, Composure, Stress Capacity, and resources.
10. Create three relationships: one trusted, one complicated, and one unfinished.

## 3.2 People, body, culture, and inheritance

Ancestry never dictates morality, class, deity loyalty, culture, gender, or profession. Use four separate layers:

| Layer | Answers |
|---|---|
| Body | What physical traits, senses, movement, resilience, or needs does the character have? |
| Heritage | Which parent race, bloodline, lineage, transformation, or created origin shaped them? |
| Culture | Who raised them, what practices did they learn, and which community claims or welcomes them? |
| Self | What name, gender, faith, identity, loyalties, and future do they choose? |

Use the current `pantheon_and_races.json` for the canonical register. Mixed heritage is ordered and specific: combine inherited traits only within the campaign's ancestry budget, then choose culture independently. The GM may reject a combination only for a clear balance or campaign-frame reason, not because the character crosses a social category.

## 3.3 Ability scores

Use one of these table-wide methods.

- Standard array: 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8.
- Point allocation: 27 points using familiar fifth-edition costs before ancestry/background adjustments.
- Rolled: roll 4d6, drop the lowest, six times; any player may use another player's array so luck does not create a weaker participant.

Background grants +2 to one ability and +1 to another, or +1 to three different abilities, maximum 17 at level 1. Ancestry does not determine ability bonuses.

## 3.4 Background

A background grants:

- two skill proficiencies;
- one tool, vehicle, language, or field proficiency;
- one community contact;
- one practical benefit that provides access rather than automatic success;
- one of the character's two starting Experiences;
- starting equipment appropriate to the campaign era.

Create backgrounds from lived roles rather than rigid careers. Examples include Archive Salvager, Ichor Clinic Attendant, Reef Advocate, Village Weatherkeeper, Faction Defector, Prison-Engine Worker, Court Interpreter, Monster-Sign Ranger, Sky-Ruin Archaeologist, or Orbital Habitat Technician.

## 3.5 Proficiencies and fields

The familiar skill list remains valid: Acrobatics, Animal Handling, Arcana, Athletics, Deception, History, Insight, Intimidation, Investigation, Medicine, Nature, Perception, Performance, Persuasion, Religion, Sleight of Hand, Stealth, and Survival.

Era-specific competence uses Field proficiencies rather than new ability scores. Common Fields include Alchemy, Computers, Engineering, Gunnery, Linguistics, Navigation, Piloting, Pressure Systems, Science, Starflight, Surgery, and Vehicle Repair. A Field pairs with whichever ability matches the approach.

## 3.6 Derived statistics

| Statistic | Formula |
|---|---|
| Proficiency Bonus | +2 levels 1–4; +3 at 5–8; +4 at 9–12; +5 at 13–16; +6 at 17–20 |
| Class save DC | 8 + PB + listed class ability modifier |
| Attack modifier | PB + relevant ability modifier |
| Passive awareness | 10 + relevant Perception or Investigation modifier |
| Composure | 8 + PB + higher of Wisdom or Charisma modifier, minimum 8 |
| Stress Capacity | 3 + PB + positive Wisdom modifier, maximum 12 |
| Guard | 0 unarmored; 1 light; 2 medium; 3 heavy; +1 shield, maximum 4 unless a feature says otherwise |
| Carry slots | 10 + Strength score; bulky items use 2–4 slots |

Guard refreshes on a Field Rest if armor can be checked and repaired. Spend 1 Guard after damage is rolled to reduce that instance by PB + the armor's Guard value. Guard cannot reduce psychic damage, suffocation, poison already inside the body, or a source the armor could not plausibly intercept.

## 3.7 Starting at level 8

The default ten-year Universal campaign may begin at level 8, but this is a campaign start point, not a level cap or a universal rule. A level-8 character completes creation at level 1, applies seven level gains in order, selects the class path at level 3, and records all feats or ability improvements. Starting wealth and contacts should reflect an established professional, not a novice with inflated statistics.

# 4. Classes, Paths, and Multiclassing

## 4.1 The twenty-two classes

Each dossier includes three selectable paths. D&D classes listed inside a dossier are transition references only and are not additional Universal classes.

## 4.2 Beat translation for existing features

The class dossiers were written using action, bonus action, movement, and reaction language. Translate them as follows.

| Existing term | Covenant Engine cost |
|---|---:|
| Movement up to Speed | 1 Beat |
| Action | 2 Beats |
| Bonus action | 1 Beat; only one feature with the Swift tag per turn |
| Reaction | Reaction |
| Free object interaction | Free once per turn |
| Action plus bonus action in one feature | 3 Beats |
| “As part of the Attack action” | Included in the 2-Beat Strike action |

Extra Attack remains part of one 2-Beat Strike; it never stacks with another Extra Attack feature. A feature that grants an additional full action grants 2 Beats, which expire at the end of the turn and cannot be used for another feature that grants extra Beats.

## 4.3 Paths

At level 3, choose one path in the class dossier.

- Melee/non-caster paths use weapons, Thundercoils, positioning, and Bounty Ichor without spell slots.
- Half-caster paths use spell ranks 1–5 and contribute half their class levels, rounded down, to multiclass slot progression after the path is chosen.
- Full-caster paths use spell ranks 1–9 and contribute class levels minus 2, minimum 0, to multiclass slot progression because casting begins at level 3.

Path identity is protected. A general feat should not duplicate a path's signature engine more efficiently than the path itself.

## 4.4 Multiclassing

To take a level in another class, have 13 in one of that class's listed primary abilities and explain how the training, awakening, bargain, adoption, or transformation occurs in the fiction. A character may have at most three classes unless the table explicitly chooses high-complexity play.

Use total character level for PB. Track class resources separately. Extra Attack does not stack. Spell slots use the contribution rules above; spells known or prepared remain class-specific. A multiclass character tracks a Duty for each class and the canonical covenant attached to each class. A bounty restores only the Bounty Ichor reserve of its own class unless a feature explicitly crosses that boundary.

## 4.5 Class balance guardrails

- A bounty trigger restores at most 1 Ichor per round and normally raises Resonance no more than once per session.
- The same creature, object, or event cannot be recycled for Ichor, Resolve, alignment, or Resonance.
- A class field is an ongoing effect; a character can maintain only one field with the same name.
- A purely protective reaction reduced to 0 Ichor still expends the Reaction.
- Thundercoil charges, heat, instability, and maintenance remain separate from Bounty Ichor.
- Concentration remains one effect per creature unless a level-21+ Legacy Gift explicitly changes it.

# 5. Deities, Ichor, and Covenants

## 5.1 Divine reality

The twenty-two gods are mechanically real and morally complicated. A character's class has exactly one canonical deity because that deity supplies the class's form of Bounty Ichor and pressure. Worship is broader: a character may honor, fear, reject, bargain with, study, or oppose any deity.

A deity cannot remove earned class levels, permanent hit points, proficiencies, or player control. Divine relationship changes access to covenant benefits, miracles, omens, bounties, and complications.

## 5.2 Resonance

Resonance measures how clearly a character and a class covenant answer one another. It runs from 0 to 6 and begins at 3.

| Score | State | Effect |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | Severed | Bounty triggers do not restore Ichor; long-rest recovery and permanent class features remain |
| 1 | Strained | First successful bounty after a Haven Rest restores no Ichor unless paired with repair or atonement |
| 2 | Distant | Class functions normally; no covenant bonus |
| 3 | Attuned | Class functions normally; omens are interpretable |
| 4 | Favored | Once per Haven Rest, fulfilling an edict at real cost grants 1 Resolve or restores 1 spent Bounty Ichor |
| 5 | Exalted | Once per Haven Rest, a valid bounty may restore 2 Ichor instead of 1 |
| 6 | Chosen | Once per chapter, request a deity-specific miracle; accepting it increases Divine Claim by 1 |

Gain Resonance by completing an edict or class bounty under meaningful stakes, normally at most once per session. Lose it by freely violating an anathema or repeatedly embodying the deity's shadow. The GM states the possible movement and reason; the player may contest factual assumptions before it is recorded.

## 5.3 Divine Claim

Claim measures how much direct access a deity has purchased, persuaded, or forced into a character's life. It runs from 0 to 6 and begins at 0 unless the player chooses otherwise.

| Score | State | Effect |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | Free | No active divine intrusion |
| 1 | Touched | Symbolic dreams or marks |
| 2 | Marked | Recognizable omens and a deity-specific Temptation |
| 3 | Whispered | Once per session, the deity may offer a complication; accepting grants 1 Resolve |
| 4 | Bound | Direct miracles may demand a visible price or obligation |
| 5 | Instrument | Refusing a direct demand costs 1 Resolve or a serious, predeclared narrative consequence |
| 6 | Threshold | Risk of avatarhood, vesselhood, or a living breach until Claim is reduced |

Claim rises when a character accepts direct miracles, bargains, shadow-driven power, or power beyond ordinary limits. It falls through costly resistance, severance rites, or choosing self-authored action when obedience would be easier.

At Claim 5 or 6, the deity still cannot choose the character's action. It can impose costs, close covenant channels, send agents, alter omens, or threaten what it can reach. The player retains the decision.

## 5.4 Ichor safety and power

Ichor is a fictional divine substance: medicine, fuel, narcotic, mutagen, sacred contaminant, and political leverage. This game provides no real-world chemistry, weapon-building, electronics, or medical instructions.

Every Ichor item has four tags:

- Source: which deity or prison system produced it.
- State: pure, stabilized, diluted, bonded, spent, or corrupted.
- Load: 0–4, measuring how much strain the item places on a user or system.
- Appetite: a short statement of the behavior it encourages or the price it seeks.

When an Ichor item is pushed beyond its rating, mark one Instability. At three Instability, it breaches, mutates, awakens, contaminates, or makes a demand appropriate to its tags. Repair clears Instability; merely resting does not.

# 6. Eight-Axis Alignment

## 6.1 The axes

Each axis runs from 0 to 3000, with 1500 as the exact pivot.

| Axis | Low | Center | High | Core question |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Altruism | Selfish | Balanced | Altruistic | Whose welfare receives priority when interests conflict? |
| Lawfulness | Chaotic | Independent | Lawful | How does the character relate to institutions, hierarchy, and procedure? |
| Cooperation | Combative | Independent | Cooperative | Do they use dominance and opposition or coordination and shared authority? |
| Honor | Dishonorable | Situational | Honorable | How reliably do they treat trust, truth, vows, surrender, and accountability? |
| Mercy | Ruthless | Tempered | Merciful | How do they treat defeated, guilty, helpless, or dangerous beings in their power? |
| Transformation | Preservative | Adaptive | Transformative | Do they preserve continuity or embrace alteration and reinvention? |
| Autonomy | Duty-Bound | Balanced | Self-Directed | Are decisions grounded in external duties or self-authored conviction and consent? |
| Restraint | Unrestrained | Measured | Disciplined | How strongly do they regulate appetite, anger, fear, ambition, power, and impulse? |

Only Altruism, Lawfulness, Cooperation, and Honor determine the 81-profile name. Mercy, Transformation, Autonomy, and Restraint form the expression line. Alignment is inner behavioral history; reputation is tracked separately.

## 6.2 Phase bands

| Range | Phase | Meaning |
|---:|---|---|
| 0–749 | Defining Low | The low endpoint repeatedly survives serious pressure |
| 750–1499 | Contested Low | The character leans low but retains common exceptions or conflict |
| 1500 | Pivot | No demonstrated directional commitment |
| 1501–2249 | Contested High | The character leans high but is still tested or developing |
| 2250–3000 | Defining High | The high endpoint repeatedly survives serious pressure |

Creation normally stays within 750–2250 unless established history supports a defining phase.

## 6.3 Movement

Alignment moves only for demonstrated behavior. Consider intent, freedom or coercion, knowledge, cost, foreseeable consequence, actual consequence, principles upheld or violated, and later repair or repetition.

| Change | Points | Use |
|---|---:|---|
| Minor | 25–100 | A meaningful but limited choice |
| Significant | 100–250 | A costly or repeated choice with visible consequence |
| Major | 250–500 | A turning point, betrayal, sacrifice, or public commitment |
| Campaign-defining | 800–1000 | A rare choice that reshapes identity and the world |

Normally award an axis at most once per scene unless separate consequential decisions occur. Movement is not XP, approval, punishment, or a command to act consistently.

## 6.4 Convictions, Ties, Duties, and Temptations

At creation, choose two Convictions: one may be Defining, and the other Major or Minor. A Conviction describes a principle the character believes. A Tie names a person, community, place, faction, deity, or ideal that matters. A Duty records an obligation created by a class, office, oath, law, or covenant. A Temptation records an attractive violation or shortcut.

Freely violating a Major or Defining Conviction may add 1 Strain. At 3 Strain, choose one: repair the breach, rewrite the Conviction, abandon it openly, or fracture it into a Temptation. The player authors the change; the world reacts to what happened.

## 6.5 Reputation is not alignment

Track Fame, Faction Standing, Cultural Honor, Legal Status, and Personal Trust separately. Only observers with credible knowledge react. A hidden act may change alignment without changing reputation. A false accusation may change reputation without changing alignment.

# 7. Scenes and Spotlight

## 7.1 Scene Modes

Use the mode that matches the pressure. Changing mode does not erase the fiction.

| Mode | Time scale | Procedure |
|---|---|---|
| Free Play | Seconds to hours | Conversation and tests as needed |
| Conflict | Six-second rounds | Initiative, three Beats, Reactions |
| Challenge | Flexible turns | Progress and danger clocks |
| Journey | Watches or days | Route choices, roles, Supply, hazard clocks |
| Downtime | Days to months | Projects, recovery, faction and settlement turns |
| Legacy | Months to years | Institutions, era change, world-scale clocks |

## 7.2 Spotlight fairness

In Free Play and Challenges, pass the spotlight when a character completes a meaningful action, a consequence demands a response, or another character is directly affected. Before giving a second consecutive spotlight to one player, check whether anyone else wants to act.

For large parties, place three spotlight tokens per player at the start of a complex scene. Spend one for each major action. A player with no tokens waits while an eligible player has tokens. Refresh all tokens when everyone has spent them or when the scene changes. Tokens track airtime, not action points.

## 7.3 Clocks

Clocks make change visible.

| Segments | Use |
|---:|---|
| 4 | Immediate obstacle, short ritual, simple chase |
| 6 | Standard investigation, dangerous journey, faction operation |
| 8 | Major project, settlement crisis, divine prison breach |
| 12 | Era shift, war, planetary threat, ten-year campaign transformation |

Use a Progress clock for what characters are building or discovering and a Danger clock for what worsens. A Clean success usually fills 1 Progress; a Breakthrough fills 2. A Costly opening may fill 1 Progress and 1 Danger. A Setback usually fills 1 Danger. A Crisis fills 2 Danger or triggers the established consequence. Fiction can change these amounts.

Clocks do not predetermine an outcome. When a clock fills, resolve the event from current choices and conditions.

# 8. Combat

## 8.1 Starting conflict

1. Establish objectives, positions, ranges, terrain, and any escape routes.
2. Determine awareness. An unaware creature has one Burden on initiative; it does not automatically lose its turn.
3. Roll initiative: d20 + Dexterity modifier, with relevant proficiency only if a feature grants it.
4. The highest result acts first. Then alternate between sides while possible. Each side chooses which eligible member uses its next slot. After every participant acts, begin a new round.

Alternating slots prevent one side from deciding the conflict before the other participates. A boss may have two or more initiative slots, but no single slot contains more than one turn.

## 8.2 Beats and Reactions

On a turn, a creature has 3 Beats and one free object interaction. It has one Reaction from the end of its turn until the start of its next turn.

| Action | Cost | Effect |
|---|---:|---|
| Step | 1 | Move up to Speed; movement may be split around actions |
| Strike | 2 | Make the attacks granted by the Attack action or use a standard offensive cantrip |
| Cast | 1–3 | Use the translated casting time: bonus action 1, action 2, longer special |
| Swift feature | 1 | Use one bonus-action feature; only one Swift feature per turn |
| Guard | 1 | Gain +2 AC until start of next turn or restore 1 spent Guard once per Field Rest |
| Disengage | 1 | Movement this turn does not trigger opportunity attacks |
| Dash | 1 | Gain extra movement equal to Speed; at most twice per turn |
| Hide | 1 | Attempt to become Hidden when cover or concealment permits |
| Assist | 1 | Give one Edge to an ally's next eligible test before your next turn |
| Interact | 1 | Manipulate a complex object, administer an item, reload a demanding weapon, or perform a brief task |
| Ready | 2 | Name a trigger and a 1- or 2-Beat action; use the Reaction when it occurs |
| Improvise | 1–3 | GM sets cost by scope |

You may repeat an action unless it has the Swift, Once, Reload, or Concentration limit. Strike includes Extra Attack, so repeating Strike is not allowed unless a feature explicitly grants an extra action or Beats.

## 8.3 Pressing a turn

Once per round, a player character may gain 1 extra Beat by marking 2 Stress. The extra Beat cannot cast a leveled spell, activate a Swift feature, or repeat Strike. A character at maximum Stress cannot Press.

## 8.4 Ranges and maps

Use a grid or range bands.

| Band | Grid guide | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| Engaged | 5 ft | Grappling, melee, immediate reach |
| Near | 10–30 ft | Same room or small deck |
| Far | 35–120 ft | Large chamber, street, field, ship section |
| Distant | 125–500 ft | Long street, battlefield, airspace |
| Remote | Beyond 500 ft | Requires sensors, special weapons, chase, or scene framing |

A normal 30-foot Speed moves from Engaged to Near, or within Near, with one Step. Moving a full band at Far or beyond may require Dash, a vehicle, or a test. Exact printed ranges win when tactical precision matters.

## 8.5 Attacks, cover, and criticals

Attack rolls target AC. A natural 20 hits and doubles all damage dice; flat modifiers are added once. A natural 1 misses. Exceeding AC by 10 is a Forceful Hit: choose one minor benefit appropriate to the attack—move the target 5 feet, deny its Reaction until its next turn, damage cover, or gain one Edge on the next action against it. A critical hit is also Forceful.

Half cover grants +2 AC and Dexterity saves. Strong cover grants +5. Total cover prevents direct targeting. Concealment normally imposes one Burden instead of changing AC.

## 8.6 Maneuvers

Any creature can attempt these through a Strike or 1-Beat setup followed by a test.

- Grapple: target chooses Strength or Dexterity save against 8 + PB + attacker's Strength modifier.
- Shove: same save; push 5 feet or knock Prone.
- Disarm: opposed attack test; on success, item lands within 5 feet. Creatures with a secure grip or integrated weapon gain one Edge.
- Pin: while grappling, spend 1 Beat and win an Athletics contest; both are Restrained until the grapple ends, but the pinner may release freely.
- Suppress: expend suitable ammunition or power to control a Near zone; crossing it requires a save or causes an opportunity attack.

## 8.7 Zones, hazards, and objectives

A strong encounter has an objective besides reducing hit points: rescue, escape, hold, disable, expose, steal, seal, negotiate, survive, or choose between costs. Terrain should offer at least two meaningful interactions and one route that changes as a clock advances.

Minions have normal defenses and actions but 1 Hit. Any damaging hit defeats a minion; a failed save against damaging area effect also defeats it. Use minions for scale, not to disguise elite enemies.

# 9. Harm, Recovery, Composure, and Death

## 9.1 Hit points and Bloodied

Hit points represent stamina, luck, guard, pain tolerance, and the ability to avoid decisive injury. At half maximum HP or fewer, a creature is Bloodied. Bloodied has no universal penalty, but features and enemy behavior may reference it.

Damage, resistance, vulnerability, immunity, temporary HP, and healing otherwise use familiar fifth-edition rules.

## 9.2 Guard and armor damage

Guard makes armor an active resource without replacing AC. Spend Guard after damage is rolled. If an attack exceeds AC by 10 or is a critical hit, it damages armor: after resolving the hit, the armor gains one Wear. At three Wear, its Guard maximum drops by 1 until repaired. At zero Guard maximum, armor still supplies AC but is compromised.

Improvised field repair clears one Wear with a DC 12 appropriate tool test and 10 minutes. A proper workshop clears all Wear during Downtime.

## 9.3 Field Rest, Haven Rest, Recuperation

| Rest | Time | Requirements | Benefits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Breather | 1 minute | No immediate attack | Spend one Hit Die or clear 1 Stress; once per Field Rest |
| Field Rest | 10 minutes | Relative safety, supplies, no combat | Spend Hit Dice; restore Guard; recover short-rest features; clear PB Stress divided among party members through care or quiet |
| Haven Rest | 8 hours | Secure shelter and at least 6 hours sleep or ancestry equivalent | Restore long-rest features and spell slots; regain half spent Hit Dice; heal to at least half HP, then spend Hit Dice; clear all ordinary Stress |
| Recuperation | 1+ days | Safety, treatment, food, and no adventuring | Heal Wounds, repair Scars when possible, treat Fractures, complete recovery projects |

A Haven Rest does not automatically restore all HP. Comfortable medical care may restore additional Hit Dice or HP. This makes safe settlements, healers, supplies, and downtime matter without forcing an attrition-heavy style.

## 9.4 Composure and Stress

Composure protects against supernatural terror, divine intrusion, identity attack, psychic contamination, and overwhelming strain. When exposed, make an appropriate save against the source's Composure DC, or roll a Composure test: d20 + PB + higher of Wisdom or Charisma modifier.

| Outcome | Stress |
|---|---:|
| Breakthrough | 0 and gain one useful insight or resistance |
| Clean success | 0 or 1 for truly overwhelming contact |
| Costly opening | Choose 1 Stress or a brief reaction that changes position or access |
| Setback | 2 Stress |
| Crisis | 3 Stress and source-specific complication |

Stress is not a diagnosis and never dictates a real-world disorder. At maximum Stress, the character is Overwhelmed: one Burden on concentration and Composure tests, and they cannot Press or voluntarily accept more Stress as a cost.

## 9.5 Fractures and Scars

If a character would take Stress beyond capacity, they choose one:

- become Incapacitated until the immediate danger passes or an ally reaches them;
- take 1d8 psychic damage per overflow Stress and remain active;
- take a Fracture and reset Stress to half capacity.

A Fracture is a temporary, player-authored response such as “Cannot trust mirrors after the dream court” or “Compulsively checks pressure seals.” It contains a Trigger, a Cost, and a Grounding method. The player portrays it. The GM may invoke its Cost at most once per scene; accepting it grants 1 Resolve. Recuperation, support, magic, or a completed recovery project can heal or rewrite it.

A Scar is a lasting change chosen at the Last Threshold or after a campaign-defining trauma. It may be bodily, magical, relational, spiritual, reputational, or technological. A Scar grants an Experience-like +2 when its hard-won lesson applies and creates a real complication when its cost applies. It is not a punishment token.

## 9.6 Zero hit points and the Last Threshold

At 0 HP, fall Prone and choose Fall or Stand.

- Fall: become Unconscious and enter the Dying track.
- Stand: remain conscious until the end of the current turn, gain one Wound, and take a final 2 Beats. Then fall Unconscious. A character can Stand only once per Haven Rest.

The Dying track has three boxes. At the start of a turn while dying, make a Constitution save, DC 10 plus current Wounds. Clean success marks no box; Breakthrough stabilizes; Costly opening marks one box but permits a final sentence or small interaction; Setback marks one; Crisis marks two. Damage at 0 marks one, or two for a critical hit. Healing removes the Dying track and restores HP normally.

When the third box would be marked, reach the Last Threshold and use the campaign's lethality mode.

## 9.7 Lethality modes

Choose at Session Zero. A player may opt into a harsher mode for their own character but not a softer mode that changes the agreed campaign stakes without discussion.

| Mode | Last Threshold choices |
|---|---|
| Heroic | Survive with a Scar; accept a divine/faction rescue with a stated Claim or debt; retire; or choose death |
| Perilous | Make a final Constitution save. On success choose Scar, rescue debt, retirement, or death; on failure choose rescue debt, retirement, or death |
| Brutal | Death occurs unless an already-established effect, immediate rescue, or resurrection applies; the player narrates the final moment |

No mode authorizes surprise sexual violence, forced identity change, or another excluded subject.

## 9.8 Resurrection and the Design of Death

Death in Universal is an administered passage, not a free reset. Resurrection requires a reachable soul, a body or true anchor when the effect requires one, consent of the deceased, and a valid method. The dead player always decides whether the soul returns.

Each return creates one Death Cost chosen collaboratively: a debt in Nefarokir's ledger, a lost or altered memory, a changed Tie, a visible death mark, a temporary reduction to maximum Hit Dice, a faction/legal complication, or a quest to repair the passage. A repeated return raises the cost or requires a rarer method; it never erases player authorship of the character.

# 10. Exploration, Investigation, and Social Play

## 10.1 Journey procedure

Define destination, purpose, known routes, travel scale, and what makes the journey uncertain. Do not use a Journey scene when travel has no interesting decision.

Choose roles. One character may hold two roles in a small party but rolls only once per watch.

| Role | Typical contribution |
|---|---|
| Guide | Route, terrain, spatial orientation |
| Scout | Hazards, ambush, signs, forward access |
| Quartermaster | Supply, rest quality, repair, load |
| Envoy | Communities, borders, law, passage |
| Specialist | Vehicle, magic, pressure, medicine, weather, stars |

Create a Progress clock and a Danger clock. Each watch, the party chooses pace: Cautious grants one Edge to hazard tests but uses 2 Supply; Steady uses 1 Supply; Urgent fills 1 Progress automatically but also fills 1 Danger and prevents a full Field Rest.

Supply is abstract. One Supply supports one character for one travel day or one party requirement such as a repair, environmental seal, medicine use, or special feed. A lack of Supply creates Exhaustion, Stress, equipment Wear, or lost time according to the fiction; it does not make food bookkeeping the only challenge.

## 10.2 Environmental layers

Use tags rather than dozens of disconnected subsystems: Heat, Cold, Wet, Pressure, Vacuum, Toxic, Corrosive, Radiation, Low Gravity, High Gravity, Unstable Ground, Supernatural Weather, and Living Terrain. Protection provides a rating from 0–3. Exposure has an intensity from 1–4. If intensity exceeds protection, make an exposure save at each meaningful interval.

WorldBuilder determines which tags are present and how they change; the rules determine what characters do about them.

## 10.3 Clue-forward investigation

An essential clue is information needed to make a meaningful choice or reach another scene. A character with a plausible approach and access finds it without rolling. A test answers one or more of these questions:

- How quickly is it found?
- How complete or precise is it?
- Is the search concealed?
- What danger is avoided?
- What extra leverage, contradiction, or weakness is uncovered?

Each important truth should exist in at least three forms: witness, record, physical trace, dream or omen, expert interpretation, enemy account, environmental change, or consequence. Destroying one source does not destroy the campaign.

Use an Evidence clock for complex cases. Breakthrough fills 2 and asks one free question. Clean success fills 1. Costly opening fills 1 with exposure, time, or a compromised source. A Setback still reveals the essential clue if the approach was competent, but fills Danger or gives the opposition time.

## 10.4 Research questions

When a clue is earned, the player may ask a question supported by the approach:

- What happened here?
- What is being concealed or misrepresented?
- Who or what had access?
- What pattern connects these facts?
- What will happen next if nobody intervenes?
- What is vulnerable, missing, out of place, or newly changed?
- Which account is least reliable, and why?

The GM answers truthfully at the level earned. A partial answer may be incomplete; it cannot be deliberately false unless the clue itself is an identified lie.

## 10.5 Social conflicts

NPCs have Needs, Fears, Boundaries, Leverage, and a starting Attitude: Hostile, Guarded, Open, Supportive, or Committed. A social roll cannot force an NPC to violate a hard Boundary, erase identity, create attraction, surrender bodily autonomy, or believe an obvious impossibility. It can change costs, timing, risk, interpretation, willingness to listen, or which option the NPC chooses.

For major negotiations, use paired 4- or 6-segment clocks: Accord and Fallout. Establish at least two possible agreements. Evidence, concessions, protection, public pressure, status, shared values, threats, and deception change effect and consequence. If Accord fills, the NPC accepts the negotiated terms they have heard. If Fallout fills, talks end, outside pressure intervenes, or the price changes.

Deception creates a hidden Truth clock. When consequences, witnesses, or contradictions fill it, the deception is exposed. The original roll determines plausibility, not permanent mind control.

## 10.6 Chases

Use a 6-segment Lead clock and a 6-segment Pursuit clock. Each round, participants choose a route and one chase action: Gain Ground, Create Obstacle, Bypass Hazard, Protect Passenger, Attack, Hide Trail, or Change Vehicle. Fill the relevant clock based on outcome bands. The quarry escapes when Lead fills; pursuers catch or force confrontation when Pursuit fills.

Offer at least two routes with different tags. A chase is about decisions and changing locations, not repeated identical speed rolls.

# 11. Downtime, Crafting, Factions, and Settlements

## 11.1 Downtime turns

A Downtime turn is normally one week, adjusted to the fiction. Each character chooses two actions, or one intensive action.

- Recover: heal a Wound, Fracture, Scar step, disease, or exhaustion.
- Build or Repair: advance a crafting or infrastructure project.
- Research: advance an Evidence or knowledge project.
- Train: begin or advance a proficiency, language, feat, or class transition.
- Connect: strengthen a Tie, contact, or community.
- Serve: work for a faction, settlement, faith, or household.
- Scheme: create leverage, cover identity, or hidden access.
- Govern: change a policy, institution, resource, or public clock.

Roll only when uncertainty and consequence remain. Otherwise spend time and resources and advance the project.

## 11.2 Projects

Every project has Scope, Requirements, a Progress clock, a Danger or Cost clock when appropriate, and a Finish effect.

| Scope | Clock | Examples |
|---|---:|---|
| Personal | 4 | Learn a language, repair rare armor, trace one lineage |
| Group | 6 | Build a workshop, cure a local blight, expose an official |
| Settlement | 8 | Establish a clinic, redesign defenses, reform a law |
| Regional | 12 | End a monopoly, build a fleet, change a divine prison function |
| Planetary or era | Linked 12s | Terraform, interplanetary network, end an Ichor economy |

Money can meet Requirements and buy tools, but it does not replace expertise, consent, rare access, or time.

## 11.3 Crafting

An item is defined by Chassis, Tier, Tags, Power Source, Load, and Quirks. A recipe is permission and understanding, not a compulsory shopping list.

To craft, meet the workshop and material Requirements, then fill Progress. On completion, choose one beneficial Quirk for a Breakthrough or accept a flaw if Danger filled first. Ichor and living technologies may develop Appetite or personality and must never be treated as inert merely because the crafter owns them.

## 11.4 Factions

Track each faction on four independent measures:

| Track | Range | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| Standing | -3 to +3 | Institutional attitude and access |
| Trust | 0 to 6 | Belief in the character's reliability |
| Heat | 0 to 6 | Urgency of scrutiny or retaliation |
| Influence | 0 to 6 | Character's ability to change faction action |

Standing is not morality. A predatory faction can love a character; an ethical institution can distrust them. Faction clocks advance when the faction has motive, knowledge, and capacity, not because the GM needs the plot restored.

## 11.5 Settlement turns

At the end of a chapter or meaningful downtime, a settlement may take one turn. Record four ratings from 0–6: Safety, Provision, Cohesion, and Autonomy. Choose one Pressure and one Response. Advance a settlement project or danger clock. Then describe one visible change in ordinary life.

Player action can improve one rating while harming another. The settlement's people choose how they respond through established leaders, factions, customs, and conflicts; they are not passive reward containers.

# 12. Equipment Across Eras

## 12.1 Era ratings

Use the WorldBuilder era scale.

| Era | Label |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Stone Age |
| 1 | Early Metallurgy |
| 2 | Iron / Classical |
| 3 | Medieval |
| 4 | Renaissance / Early Modern |
| 5 | Industrial / Steam |
| 6 | Electrified / Modern |
| 7 | Digital / Atomic |
| 8 | Planetary / Orbital |
| 9 | Interplanetary |
| 10 | Spacefaring / Interstellar |

Era measures common access, infrastructure, training, replacement parts, and social assumptions. It does not measure personal worth or automatic combat superiority. A relic, spell, divine organ, or advanced visitor can exceed local Era.

## 12.2 Function profiles

Build weapons from function rather than historical name.

| Profile | Damage | Properties |
|---|---:|---|
| Light | 1d6 | Concealable, finesse or thrown |
| Standard | 1d8 | One-handed or versatile |
| Heavy | 1d10 | Two-handed, forceful |
| Great | 2d6 | Two-handed, bulky |
| Sidearm | 1d8 | Ranged, Near/Far, reload |
| Longarm | 1d10 | Ranged, Far/Distant, two-handed, reload |
| Scatter | 2d6 | Near, two-handed, reload; one Burden at Far |
| Precision | 1d12 | Far/Distant, aim, two-handed, reload |

A sword, vibroblade, fossil-tooth macuahuitl, and bounded plasma cutter can use the same profile with different tags. Superior technology changes access, range, armor interaction, sensors, maintenance, and Scale before it changes bounded personal damage.

## 12.3 Tags

Common tags include Aim, Arc, Automatic, Blast, Breach, Concealable, Defensive, Finesse, Forceful, Heavy, Integrated, Nonlethal, Reach, Reload, Silent, Thrown, Two-Handed, Unstable, and Versatile.

- Aim: spend 1 Beat without moving to gain one Edge on the next attack this turn.
- Automatic: spend 1 Supply or charge to Suppress a Near zone.
- Blast: affects a Near point and adjacent Engaged targets; targets save for half if the effect permits.
- Breach: counts as one Scale higher against objects, cover, and vehicles, not creatures.
- Defensive: while wielded, Guard action also grants +1 Guard until next turn.
- Forceful: on a Forceful Hit, push 10 feet instead of 5.
- Reload: after a number of attacks set by the item, spend 1 Beat and ammunition/charge.
- Unstable: a Crisis adds one Wear or Instability.

## 12.4 Armor profiles

| Armor | Base AC | Guard | Common limits |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Light | 11 + Dex | 1 | Minimal |
| Medium | 13 + Dex, max +2 | 2 | Stealth Burden for some suits |
| Heavy | 16 | 3 | Strength or power requirement; Stealth Burden |
| Shield | +2 AC | +1 | Occupies hand or mount |
| Powered shell | 16–18 | 3 | Requires charge, maintenance, and Era access |

Specific class dossiers or items may use familiar fifth-edition armor values. Choose one calculation; do not stack base AC formulas.

## 12.5 Wealth, Availability, and Supply

Use familiar coinage for ordinary purchases where it helps, but rare gear requires Availability as well as price.

| Availability | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Common | Ordinary local purchase |
| Controlled | License, guild, faction, or professional access |
| Restricted | Mission, black market, state, temple, or military authority |
| Unique | Project, discovery, patron, or story reward |

Supply abstracts ammunition, charge packs, consumable components, ordinary spare parts, and expedition necessities. A character carries PB Supply without using slots; extra Supply uses one carry slot each.

# 13. Vehicles, Voyages, and Starships

## 13.1 Shared vehicle chassis

Every mount, wagon, ship, submarine, skyship, aircraft, orbital craft, and starship uses the same statistics.

- Scale 0–5.
- Hull points and Hull Dice.
- Defense and Armor.
- Speed and Handling.
- Systems: Drive, Control, Sensors, Life Support, Weapons, and Special.
- Stations and Crew requirement.
- Strain and Breaches.

| Scale | Example scope |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Personal mount, bike, tiny skiff, exosuit |
| 1 | Wagon, car, launch, small airship |
| 2 | Train engine, patrol ship, bomber, corvette |
| 3 | Ocean liner, major skyship, frigate, habitat section |
| 4 | Dreadnought, city-ship, orbital fortress |
| 5 | Megastructure, world-engine, divine prison complex |

## 13.2 Scale

For each Scale of difference, the larger side gains one Edge on actions where mass, reach, armor, or output matters. At two or more Scale difference, personal weapons cannot damage Hull unless they have Breach, target an exposed system, enter the larger structure, or exploit a discovered weakness. Larger weapons may automatically destroy unprotected smaller objects, but named characters receive a save or consequence choice when the fiction permits.

## 13.3 Stations

| Station | Common actions |
|---|---|
| Command | Coordinate, Rally, set objective, negotiate |
| Helm | Maneuver, evade, pursue, dock, land |
| Engineering | Route power, repair, vent Strain, overdrive |
| Sensors | Scan, target, jam, navigate, interpret environment |
| Weapons | Fire, suppress, intercept, breach |
| Operations | Cargo, medicine, passengers, boarding, special systems |

A character at a station uses their own abilities and relevant Field. An unstaffed required station imposes one Burden or disables its actions.

## 13.4 Vehicle conflict

Each vehicle turn has 3 Command Beats shared among staffed stations, plus one Reaction for the vehicle. Each station may act at most once per round unless a feature says otherwise. Personal turns may occur inside or around the vehicle at the same time.

Damage first reduces temporary Shields if present, then Hull. When a vehicle loses one quarter of maximum Hull in one hit or takes a critical hit, mark a Breach. Choose or roll an affected system. At three Breaches, it is Disabled; at five, it is Destroyed or catastrophically failing. Occupants get time to respond unless instant destruction was an agreed and clearly telegraphed risk.

## 13.5 Voyages

Long voyages use Journey rules at the correct scale. A starship's “route” may be an orbital window, current, gate sequence, dream corridor, or interstellar transit solution. The rules do not require fixed setting coordinates. WorldBuilder can supply distances and environmental tags when that canon is ready.

# 14. Magic, Technology, and Scale

## 14.1 Source and effect

Every extraordinary effect has a Source tag and one or more Effect tags.

Sources: Arcane, Divine, Primal, Psionic, Ichor, Biological, Chemical, Mechanical, Digital, Stellar, Planar, or Hybrid.

Effects: Attack, Control, Create, Detect, Heal, Move, Protect, Summon, Transform, Communicate, or Travel.

Source determines what can disrupt, detect, fuel, corrupt, or legally regulate the effect. Effect determines what it does. A technological invisibility field and illusion spell may both Conceal, but only the spell is automatically subject to antimagic and only the device is automatically subject to power loss or electronic warfare.

## 14.2 Countering effects

A counter must match a vulnerability.

- Antimagic counters Arcane, Divine, Primal, and some Planar effects as stated.
- Wards counter named Sources, creatures, or Effect tags.
- Dispel removes an ongoing magical effect; it does not erase a mundane consequence the magic already caused.
- Electronic warfare counters Digital sensors, control, or communication.
- Engineering counters Mechanical systems.
- Medicine, antitoxin, or bio-control counters Biological and Chemical effects.
- Ichor grounding, dilution, sealing, or covenant action counters Ichor according to the item's state.

Hybrid effects require a counter to at least one essential Source. The GM states what a successful counter can achieve before a player spends a scarce resource.

## 14.3 Spellcasting

Use the class dossier's schools, casting ability, spell catalog, preparation, and progression. Rank is synonymous with spell level in this book. Concentration, components, range, duration, attacks, and saves remain in force.

When an old spell assumes a medieval object or environment, preserve its mechanical purpose and translate the expression. A spell that manipulates a door can affect an equivalent hatch; one that targets a beast does not automatically target a synthetic organism unless its tags say Beast or Biological and the conversion is fair.

## 14.4 Rituals

A ritual is a Challenge with Requirements, a Progress clock, and a Danger clock. Participants take roles, spend components or access, and make meaningful choices. A ritual can reproduce a known ritual spell, extend scale or duration, combine sources, change a divine prison function, open long-distance passage, or accomplish a unique effect.

Large effects require large consequences, infrastructure, time, consent, rare leverage, or multiple completed projects. A single high roll does not bypass the agreed scope.

## 14.5 Thundercoils

Thundercoils are optional equipment. They follow normal weapon proficiency and attack rules. Track Charge, Heat, Instability, Maintenance, and any Ichor Appetite separately from class Bounty Ichor.

- A standard discharge spends 1 Charge.
- An Overload improves one damage die step, range band, or area, then adds 1 Heat.
- At Heat 3, further Overload adds 1 Instability and the weapon cannot clear Heat without a Field Rest and tools.
- A Crisis on an Unstable Thundercoil creates a breach appropriate to its source and surroundings.

Class features can travel through a Thundercoil attack only when the dossier permits it. This never grants free Charge or Overload.

# 15. Advancement and Legacy Ranks

## 15.1 Levels 1–20

Use milestone advancement by default. The party advances when it has completed, transformed, abandoned with consequence, or decisively reframed enough major objectives to change its capabilities. Refusing the prepared quest does not block advancement; pursuing a player-created objective can qualify.

For XP play, use the familiar cumulative thresholds supplied in the current fifth-edition guide. Award XP for objectives, discoveries, rescues, negotiations, projects, hazards, and meaningful combat—not for killing alone. Everyone who participates in a chapter receives equal base XP.

## 15.2 Growth marks

At the end of a session, mark one Growth on a skill, Field, Experience, Tie, or project when it succeeded under meaningful stakes or a failure taught something costly. At three Growth, choose one:

- rewrite the item to reflect what changed;
- gain one Edge the next time it is central;
- begin a downtime training project toward proficiency or Expertise;
- improve an Experience at a tier boundary if the level rules allow.

Growth never raises ability scores or class level by itself.

## 15.3 Feats and ability improvements

At a class level granting an Ability Score Improvement, choose one:

- +2 to one ability;
- +1 to two abilities;
- one full feat;
- two minor talents approved by the GM.

Ability scores normally cap at 20 before Legacy Ranks. A feat converted from another fifth-edition source must use the Beat translation and cannot create an infinite resource or repeated Strike loop.

## 15.4 Legacy Ranks 21–30

After character level 20, advancement becomes ten Legacy Ranks rather than additional class levels. PB remains +6. Each rank grants one Legacy Gift from an allowed category; a category cannot be chosen at consecutive ranks unless the gift says repeatable.

| Rank | Gift |
|---:|---|
| 21 | Ability cap +2 and one ability +2, or Epic feat |
| 22 | Mastery: Expertise in two skills/Fields or one new major proficiency |
| 23 | Covenant Gift tied to Resonance or a completed severance |
| 24 | Resilience: extra Wound capacity, Composure, or Guard option |
| 25 | Domain: establish or transform a group-scale institution, vessel, sanctum, or network |
| 26 | Apex improvement to one class engine, approved against its dossier |
| 27 | Scale Gift: act one Scale higher for one narrow purpose |
| 28 | Legendary ritual, invention, or relationship authority |
| 29 | Second Epic feat or Ability cap +2 |
| 30 | Legacy Choice: apotheosis, mortality, office, voyage, transformation, retirement, or player-authored equivalent |

Legacy Gifts expand scope more often than numbers. They should create new decisions rather than make ordinary party members irrelevant.

# 16. GM Framework

## 16.1 Session Zero

Agree on:

- era and allowed technology;
- starting level and advancement method;
- Heroic, Perilous, or Brutal lethality;
- horror intensity and Composure use;
- lines, veils, pause tool, and check-in method;
- divine coercion boundaries and character-specific forbidden transformations;
- expected campaign length, party size, and scheduling;
- whether alignment scores are public, private, or shared only during reviews;
- rules for player-versus-player conflict, secrets, theft, persuasion, and romance;
- how WorldBuilder and LifeSimulation information enters play.

## 16.2 Preparing a chapter

Prepare situations, not required scenes.

1. State the Pressure: what is changing without the characters?
2. Give three Hooks connected to different player interests.
3. Place each essential truth in at least three sources.
4. Prepare at least four approaches: social, investigative, covert, ritual/technical, and direct where relevant; accept a sixth created by players.
5. Give every major faction a Need, Fear, Plan, Capacity, and Limit.
6. Create one Progress and one Danger clock.
7. List several possible resolutions and their honest costs; leave room for an unforeseen one.
8. Ask which unresolved player Tie or Conviction can be invited, not compelled.

## 16.3 Consequence ladder

Use the lightest consequence that follows from the established risk.

1. Reveal trouble or a hard choice.
2. Spend time, Supply, position, secrecy, or opportunity.
3. Add Stress, Wear, Instability, or faction Heat.
4. Advance a Danger clock or separate allies.
5. Inflict damage, a condition, a Wound, or loss of access.
6. Change a relationship, institution, region, or divine state.

Never use a consequence merely to restore the planned plot.

## 16.4 Encounter threat budget

For a quick first pass, set a budget in Threat Points (TP). Each player character contributes 4 TP for a Standard conflict, 3 for a Light conflict, 5 for a Hard conflict, or 6 for an Extreme conflict.

Rate enemies relative to party level.

| Enemy | TP |
|---|---:|
| Minion or four+ levels lower | 1 |
| Minor, two–three levels lower | 2 |
| Peer, within one level | 4 |
| Elite, two levels higher or with two strong turns | 7 |
| Boss, three+ levels higher or multi-phase | 10–16 |

Add 1–4 TP for severe terrain, an advancing ritual, protected civilians, or another objective that consumes actions. Subtract 1–4 for strong allied support or a decisive prepared advantage. This is a playtest calibration tool: creature accuracy, control, area damage, and action count matter more than the printed label.

## 16.5 Bosses

A boss should have multiple decision points, not inflated HP alone. Use two initiative slots, telegraphed reactions, breakable defenses, phase changes, environmental control, and a non-damage objective. Never give a boss unlimited interrupts. Each reaction names a trigger and cost.

## 16.6 Information and secrets

Secret notes can create delight, but essential campaign understanding cannot depend on one player remembering to reveal one note. Distinguish player knowledge from character knowledge without forcing players to perform ignorance in ways that make play worse. If dramatic irony is fun, use it openly.

## 16.7 Safety and agency in horror

Describe sensory and supernatural pressure, then return authorship of internal response to the player. The GM may offer impulses or reactions; the player chooses how the character experiences them unless a short condition explicitly applies. Avoid real-diagnosis stereotypes. A Fracture is a game-state consequence and story prompt, not a claim about mental illness.

# 17. WorldBuilder and LifeSimulation Bridge

## 17.1 Ownership boundary

WorldBuilder owns terrain, maps, planetary geometry, environment tags, era state, locations, and physical world simulation. LifeSimulation owns NPC identity, schedules, reactions, conversations, relationships, and social consequences. The Covenant Engine owns tests, resources, clocks, conflict, harm, advancement, alignment, covenant state, and campaign consequence.

No system silently overwrites another system's authority.

## 17.2 Shared state objects

| Object | Required fields |
|---|---|
| Character | id, level, classes, abilities, proficiencies, HP, Guard, Stress, alignment, covenants, ties |
| NPC | id, location, schedule state, needs, fears, boundaries, attitude, faction, relationship, current reaction |
| Scene | mode, participants, environment tags, era, scale, progress clocks, danger clocks |
| Location | semantic id, biome tags, hazard tags, settlement rating, controlling factions |
| Faction | standing, trust, heat, influence, plan clocks, known information |
| Vehicle | scale, hull, systems, stations, strain, breaches, power source |
| Campaign thread | hooks, lore sources, resolutions, clocks, status, consequences |

## 17.3 Event contract

The engine may emit events such as `test_resolved`, `clock_changed`, `relationship_changed`, `alignment_reviewed`, `resonance_changed`, `claim_changed`, `npc_reaction_requested`, `settlement_turn_completed`, `era_changed`, and `vehicle_breached`.

WorldBuilder and LifeSimulation may propose tags and consequences, but the GM confirms mechanical changes. Dialogue generation cannot spend player resources, move alignment, accept a divine bargain, or speak for a player character.

## 17.4 NPC reactions

LifeSimulation should derive an NPC reaction from knowledge, relationship, schedule, current need, faction pressure, and witnessed action. It must not read inner alignment as public fact unless the NPC has a credible magical or institutional method. Reactions can change Personal Trust or faction Heat; the GM confirms the final rating.

## 17.5 Era transitions

An era change is a Legacy-scale project, not a slider that instantly rewrites every settlement. Track Discovery, Infrastructure, Access, and Social Adoption separately. A settlement can use Era 8 orbital medicine while farming at Era 3, or maintain Era 5 steam systems beside divine technology. WorldBuilder's global era is the common ceiling, not a compulsory uniform culture.

# 18. Ten-Year Campaign Autonomy

## 18.1 Timeline status

Every “should” in the ten-year plan means “likely if the players pursue this thread.” Years and months are pacing windows, not scheduled outcomes. The GM may combine, delay, reorder, extend, or omit them in response to interest and fallout.

Players may ignore, refuse, bargain with, ally with, redeem, bind, exile, expose, transform, replace, contain, postpone, or destroy any divine threat. Consequences follow choices but never secretly correct them back to canon.

## 18.2 Hook, lore, quest, consequence

| Stage | Rule |
|---|---|
| Hook | Invite attention through a visible consequence, request, contradiction, rumor, omen, or opportunity connected to current goals |
| Lore | Place important truth in at least three independent forms |
| Quest | Offer multiple approaches and accept a player-created approach |
| Consequence | Advance the world honestly from the chosen action, including refusal or delay |

A valid hook can be declined without ending the campaign. A valid mystery can be understood through more than one NPC. A valid quest can be reframed. A valid consequence respects what the party actually changed.

## 18.3 Ten default themes

| Year | Theme | Suggested pressure, not required result |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Threads of Peace | Civic corruption, peacekeeping, containment clues, ordinary work touching divine machinery |
| 2 | First Godfall Engines | Created minds, public works, machine cults, inherited obedience |
| 3 | Hearth Rot and Tide Hunger | Food, disease, care, wetlands, reefs, dependency, communal survival |
| 4 | War Crown and Dragon Law | Occupation, sovereignty, command, resistance, conquest |
| 5 | Origin World Revelation | Archives, astronomy, psionic proof, thresholds, ownership of truth |
| 6 | Sea Sun and Broken Horizon | Storm, reef, sky, prophecy, weather control, terraforming |
| 7 | Lineage Moonwood and Forge Ash | Ancestry, family law, wilderness, labor, craft, consent |
| 8 | Dream Beast and Beautiful Lie | Desire, dream, beauty, instinct, engineered identity, consent |
| 9 | Shadow Titan and Ledgerless Dead | Death, memory, burden, transformation, funeral bureaucracy |
| 10 | The Final Hunger | Adaptation, mutation, survival, reconstruction, divine feeding ecology |

## 18.4 Open resolutions

Prepare costs for alliance, reform, exposure, severance, binding, exile, mortal replacement, redemption, transformation, destruction, containment, postponement, and deliberate nonintervention. Then follow the players' actual plan. A year title is a theme, never a guaranteed casualty list.

## 18.5 Autonomy audit

Before a chapter, ask:

- Can the players say no and still have a campaign?
- Can they learn enough through more than one path?
- Are preserve, alter, expose, negotiate, leave, and end genuinely possible where the fiction permits?
- Does a prophecy describe pressure rather than declare a player choice?
- Will a class duty create an offer or cost instead of a compulsory act?
- Will alignment record behavior rather than reward compliance?
- If the party surprises me, are my factions able to respond instead of resetting the situation?

# 19. Conditions and Quick Reference

## 19.1 Conditions

Use familiar fifth-edition conditions with these clarifications and additions.

| Condition | Effect |
|---|---|
| Blinded | Cannot see; attacks have one Burden; attacks against you have one Edge; sight-dependent actions fail |
| Charmed | Cannot attack or directly harm the source; source has one Edge on social tests; does not control decisions or create attraction |
| Deafened | Cannot hear; hearing-dependent actions fail |
| Exhausted | Rating 1–6; subtract rating from d20 tests and reduce Speed by 5 feet per two ratings; death at 6 |
| Frightened | One Burden on tests while source is perceptible; cannot willingly move closer unless you spend 1 Beat bracing |
| Grappled | Speed 0; ends when grappler is unable to hold or target escapes |
| Hidden | Unseen and location uncertain; ends through exposure, detection, or obvious action |
| Incapacitated | Cannot spend Beats or Reactions; concentration ends |
| Invisible | Cannot be seen without a special sense; does not automatically hide sound, tracks, heat, scent, or disturbance |
| Overwhelmed | Cannot Press; one Burden on concentration and Composure tests |
| Paralyzed | Incapacitated; Speed 0; Strength and Dexterity saves fail; close hits are critical |
| Petrified | Transformed into inert substance; Incapacitated, resistance to damage, immune poison/disease, does not age |
| Poisoned | One Burden on attacks and ability tests |
| Prone | Crawling costs double; standing costs 1 Beat; close attacks gain Edge, distant attacks gain Burden |
| Restrained | Speed 0; attacks have Burden; attacks against gain Edge; Dexterity saves have Burden |
| Stunned | Incapacitated, Speed 0, Strength and Dexterity saves have Burden; repeat save at end of turn when effect permits |
| Unconscious | Incapacitated, unaware, Prone, drops held items; close hits are critical |

## 19.2 One-page play loop

1. GM describes situation, pressure, and obvious options.
2. Player states intent and approach.
3. If outcome is certain or failure is boring, resolve without a roll.
4. Otherwise set effect, risk, DC, Edge/Burden, and relevant proficiency.
5. Roll and read the outcome band.
6. Player may spend Resolve or Push when eligible.
7. Apply consequence that follows from the stated risk.
8. Update clocks, resources, relationships, covenant, or alignment only when triggered.
9. Pass spotlight.

## 19.3 Combat turn card

- 3 Beats.
- Step 1; Strike 2; Swift 1; Guard 1; Disengage 1; Dash 1; Hide 1; Assist 1; Interact 1; Ready 2.
- One free object interaction.
- One Reaction between the end of this turn and start of next.
- Press once per round: mark 2 Stress for 1 restricted Beat.
- Spend Guard after damage: reduce by PB + Guard value.
- At 0 HP: Fall or Stand.

## 19.4 End-of-session review

- Which clocks changed, and why?
- Which faction or settlement learned what?
- Did a Conviction, Tie, Duty, or Temptation create a meaningful cost and Resolve?
- Did behavior justify alignment movement?
- Did an edict, anathema, bargain, or bounty change Resonance or Claim?
- Did everyone receive meaningful spotlight?
- What consequence is now visible, and which hook is optional next?

# 20. Conversion and Playtest Notes

## 20.1 Fifth-edition conversion

| Printed rule | Conversion |
|---|---|
| Advantage/disadvantage | One Edge/one Burden |
| Action | 2 Beats |
| Bonus action | 1 Beat, Swift |
| Movement | Step, 1 Beat |
| Short rest | Field Rest; features recover once the 10-minute rest completes |
| Long rest | Haven Rest; features recover, but HP follows this book's rest rule |
| Spell level | Spell rank |
| Heroic Inspiration | Convert to 1 Resolve, respecting maximum 3 |
| Madness or sanity loss | Use Composure, Stress, Fracture, and Scar |
| Alignment prerequisite | Translate to one or more axis thresholds and demonstrated conduct |
| Vehicle stat block | Add Scale, Systems, Stations, Strain, and Breaches |

## 20.2 Converting action-heavy features

If a feature was balanced around one action and one bonus action, it normally costs all 3 Beats. If a feature grants an action, grant 2 temporary Beats. If it grants movement, grant a free Step with the stated restrictions. A feature cannot create more than one extra Strike per turn unless it explicitly represents a level-17+ apex and has a limited use.

## 20.3 Converting creatures

Keep AC, HP, ability scores, saves, attacks, damage, resistances, and spell DCs. Translate actions by cost. Give a standard creature 3 Beats; its Multiattack is a 2-Beat Strike. Give a legendary creature extra initiative slots or telegraphed Reactions instead of unrestricted legendary actions. Convert lair actions to a visible environment clock or a fixed end-of-round event.

## 20.4 Playtest flags

The following rules require table data and should be reviewed every three sessions:

- whether three Beats allow too much movement or too many defensive stacks;
- Guard reduction at each tier;
- Stress Capacity and the cost of Press;
- encounter Threat Points for parties larger than six;
- vehicle Scale interactions and Hull damage;
- Legacy Gifts above level 20;
- Haven Rest healing pace;
- frequency of Resolve, Resonance, and alignment movement.

Change one variable at a time. Record the old rule, new rule, reason, start date, and affected characters. Do not retroactively punish choices made under an earlier version.

## 20.5 Canon and compatibility statement

This is an unofficial homebrew rules system for the Universal setting. It is not an official Dungeons & Dragons, Pathfinder, Call of Cthulhu, or Daggerheart product. Names used in the design genealogy identify the traditions examined in the user-supplied research files. The Covenant Engine's procedures are original implementations written for Universal. Existing third-party or official content remains subject to its own license and is not reproduced here.

## 20.6 Final table principle

Rules exist to make choices clear, costs meaningful, characters distinct, and consequences trustworthy. When a rule would erase a reasonable choice without adding safety, clarity, or dramatic weight, pause and repair the rule. Universal can be dangerous, hungry, divine, and vast without becoming a machine that plays the characters for their players.

lines.text: # D&D 5.5e: Universal Edition
## Unofficial Homebrew Playtest Rulebook — Covenant Engine v1.0

This is a complete campaign engine for Universal. It uses a familiar fifth-edition d20 chassis while rebuilding the parts that need to carry investigation, horror, social consequence, living factions, divine pressure, ancient eras, industrial play, planetary travel, and interstellar play. The attached twenty-two Universal class dossiers remain the authority for class features. This book supplies the shared rules those classes use.

Universal is warm, wet, crowded, engineered, divine, rotten, and hungry. Its gods are creators, predators, patrons, prisoners, and sources of Ichor. Its people are not defined by their creators. Its campaign future is not defined by an outline. The rules therefore make choices legible and consequential without using mechanics to force a choice.

> Core promise. The world reacts honestly. The gods may tempt, threaten, bargain, or collect a price. Factions may remember and retaliate. Alignment may record a pattern. None of those things chooses a player character's action for them.
### Contents
1. The Covenant Engine
2. Core Resolution
3. Character Creation
4. Classes, Paths, and Multiclassing
5. Deities, Ichor, and Covenants
6. Eight-Axis Alignment
7. Scenes and Spotlight
8. Combat
9. Harm, Recovery, Composure, and Death
10. Exploration, Investigation, and Social Play
11. Downtime, Crafting, Factions, and Settlements
12. Equipment Across Eras
13. Vehicles, Voyages, and Starships
14. Magic, Technology, and Scale
15. Advancement and Legacy Ranks
16. GM Framework
17. WorldBuilder and LifeSimulation Bridge
18. Ten-Year Campaign Autonomy
19. Conditions and Quick Reference
20. Conversion and Playtest Notes
# 1. The Covenant Engine
## 1.1 What this system keeps

The system keeps the parts of modern fifth-edition fantasy play that make characters readable and portable: six ability scores, d20 tests, proficiency bonus, Armor Class, hit points, Hit Dice, saving throws, spell ranks 1–9, concentration, resistance, vulnerability, class levels, subclasses, feats, and the level 1–20 proficiency curve.

It also keeps the existing Universal class contract. Every class has a hit die, primary abilities, two saving throw proficiencies, a canonical deity, a Bounty Ichor reserve, a core class engine, and three paths: melee/non-caster, half-caster, and full-caster. A class dossier wins if a specific feature conflicts with a general rule in this book.
## 1.2 What this system changes
The Covenant Engine adds or replaces the following shared procedures.
| Need | Universal rule |
| More expressive d20 results | Five outcome bands, declared stakes, and an optional Push |
| Flexible turns | Three Beats plus one Reaction, with a compatibility translation for action and bonus-action features |
| Better investigations | Essential clues are found by competent approaches; rolls decide speed, clarity, safety, and extra leverage |
| Player-facing moral growth | Eight behavioral axes, Convictions, Ties, Resolve, Strain, Resonance, and Divine Claim |
| Horror without loss-of-agency caricatures | Composure, Stress, Fractures, and player-authored Scars |
| Living threats and projects | Visible or concealed 4-, 6-, 8-, and 12-segment clocks |
| Play across history and space | Era and Scale tags that change access and fiction without rewriting core math |
| Meaningful armor and defenses | AC prevents hits; Guard lets armor absorb a limited amount of harm |
| Less arbitrary death | A Session Zero lethality mode and explicit Last Threshold choices |
| Campaign autonomy | Hooks, redundant lore, multiple approaches, open resolutions, and honest consequence |
## 1.3 Design genealogy
This game borrows the purpose of useful mechanics, then implements that purpose in its own way.
| Source tradition | Purpose retained | Covenant Engine implementation |
| Fifth-edition fantasy | Fast d20 familiarity, bounded numbers, class identity | Familiar statistics, PB curve, AC/HP, saves, spells, and levels |
| Tactical d20 fantasy | Flexible action use, degrees of outcome, clear modes of play | Three Beats, outcome bands, and Scene Modes |
| Investigative horror | Clues, escalating risk, pushes, long-term psychological cost | Clue-forward tests, Pushes, Composure, Fractures, and Scars |
| Narrative heroic fantasy | Spotlight fairness, player currency, clocks, identity phrases | Spotlight checks, Resolve, clocks, Convictions, Ties, and Experiences |
No rule requires dice when the result is certain or when failure would add nothing. Say yes, state the cost, or ask for a test only when the outcome can change the situation.
## 1.4 Rules priority
Apply rules in this order:
1. The group's Session Zero agreements and safety boundaries.
2. A specific class, ancestry, spell, item, creature, or scene rule.
3. This core rulebook.
4. A fifth-edition-compatible source converted using Chapter 20.
5. A fair table ruling that is recorded if it will recur.

A later canon package supersedes an older one on the same subject. For this edition, the Eight-Axis Covenant Alignment package supersedes older four-axis alignment text inside the life compendium. The newest twenty-two-class package governs classes. Current pantheon and race JSON governs names, creator categories, and deity relationships.
